items.title: George Wein interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2001
items.q: And later on I studied with Teddy Wilson, when I was in college in my junior year. I came to New York and studied with him at Juilliard.

ctx.x: I have a very short quote from the All Music Guide to Jazz, who describes you as “an Earl Hines-influenced pianist.” © Fiillius Jazz Archive -6-

Sam Sax, my teacher, was a disciple of Earl Hines. And in those days of course you didn’t have Bud Powell stamps. Earl Hines was the piano player for the big bands. I loved Teddy Wilson and Earl Hines. Teddy Wilson was a refined version of Earl Hines. Earl Hines played with octaves and tremolos. Teddy played single finger. But they had the same basic approach to the music, the same melodic approach. And so I loved both of those players. And later on I studied with Teddy Wilson, when I was in college in my junior…

He went to the race track every afternoon. He did his work in the morning and made enough money to support the house and lost the rest to the races. For 25 years. But it saved his life. items.title: 66600_Teddy Wilson oral history interview
items.q: I worked with George all over South America, Vienna, Spain, France, Holland, all over Europe

ctx.x: and Buddy Rich. Ray Brown. That carried the banner of jazz all over the world. They made a tremendous [impression], in Europe and Japan.

So you got to give Norman GranZ some credit. But I would say those three -- Norman GranZ and George Wein started his festival, the Newport Festival of 1954, and now he's presented jazz all over the world. I worked with George all over South America, Vienna, Spain, France, Holland, all over Europe -- New Orleans, etc.
I played with you at Newport once.

items.title: George Wein — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: And I said, "I'm going to bring all the great players over, 'cause they were all still alive: Earl Hines, Teddy Wilson."

ctx.x: Multiple stages, simultaneously. A logistics nightmare I can only imagine. And I think, correct me if I'm wrong here, you were also somehow kind of got involved in booking beyond the Festival, which served some benefit to you in getting guys over to Nice in the first place.

It's funny about life, because what I'm doing now is totally different from what I did at Nice. Because in Europe, at that time, there were a lot of avant garde festivals happening. Nobody was paying attention to traditional jazz. And I said, "I'm going to bring all the great players over, 'cause they were all still alive: Earl Hines, Teddy Wilson." Nobody cared about them anymore. They were all into either (post?), Coltrane was already big by 74, and you had these festivals in Germany, and you'd read the papers…
Did you ever make money in Nice?
